title: Articles of Note: Week of September 7, 2026
author: Jason Moore
summary: This is Jason Moore's weekly curated digest of classical-education and K-12 commentary, presented with a one- or two-paragraph excerpt and source credit for each linked piece. The strongest through-line is a defense of classical education against two pressures: modern scientism (Classical Baccalaureate's piece on teaching science within a classical framework) and technological/AI encroachment (Gary Houchens's essay on Paul Kingsnorth's 'the Machine' and whom AI actually serves). Several entries document a broader crisis narrative -- record-low humanities degree completions, a 27-year-low in Gallup's K-12 satisfaction numbers, and PISA 2025 scores at their lowest ever for OECD countries -- that the roundup implicitly reads as evidence for the classical-education critique of modern schooling. John Mark Reynolds's excerpt argues that classical education is inseparable from rooted, multigenerational community, illustrated through a family Bible passed down four generations. The digest closes with a run of 9/11 twenty-fifth-anniversary pieces, several with clear educational angles (how the attacks are taught as lived memory fades, a 9/11-vs-COVID comparison of educational policy responses) and others more personal or elegiac. Taken as a whole, the roundup functions as Moore's weekly argument that the data trends in American education validate the classical model's core complaints.
points: The roundup pairs Gary Houchens's essay on Paul Kingsnorth's 'the Machine' with Gregory Wilbur's piece on music and order, framing classical education as a counterweight to both technological and cultural disorder.
It flags that U.S. colleges awarded only 164,847 undergraduate humanities degrees in 2025 -- the smallest number since 1991 and nearly a third below the 2012 peak.
It cites a Walton Family Foundation/Gallup poll putting American satisfaction with K-12 schools at 32%, the lowest in Gallup's 27-year trend, with dissatisfaction at a record 67%.
It excerpts John Mark Reynolds's argument that classical education requires rooted, multigenerational community, illustrated by a family Bible carried across four generations.
The digest notes PISA 2025 recorded the lowest-ever average OECD scores in reading, science and mathematics, with Finland's scores now trailing Australia's.
quotes: As you survey the weeds in the flowerbeds, the length of the grass in your yard, the rising stacks of dishes or mounds of laundry, there exists an urge to set things right and push against the chaos. That innate impulse is to bring order.

The Machine" is Kingsnorth's metaphor for the global techno-economic system that has brought an unprecedented quality of material life to humankind but has nearly destroyed us spiritually, psychologically, and socially.
U.S. colleges awarded 164,847 undergraduate humanities degrees in 2025. That's the smallest number since 1991 and nearly a third below 2012 levels, the most recent peak, according to the academy.

I sometimes read from my great-grandfather's Bible. Lewis Dayton Reynolds (LDR) outlined his sermons in the book, which was small enough to fit in his saddlebag as he rode from church to church in West Virginia.
That "satisfaction" poll figure — 32% — is reportedly the lowest in Gallup's 27-year trend, and it's down 11% over the past two years.

It is now time to stop lauding Finland as the land of educational miracles. Stratospheric scores in 2005 have been followed by almost relentless decline. Finland now posts lower scores than Australia, albeit with the saving grace that the difference is not a significant one.
